purpose: Provide full literary situations for operator comparisons whose value lies in care, access, distributed growth, building and release rather than isolated keywords.

scenes.title: Hosea's parent-child image: teaching Ephraim to walk while carrying and healing
scenes.scene_type: prophetic parental metaphor / judgment and compassion
scenes.summary: Hosea depicts YHWH's relation to Israel with parental imagery: calling a child from Egypt, teaching Ephraim to walk, taking them in the arms, drawing them with cords of kindness and bending down to feed them. The tenderness is set against Israel's refusal and the threat of judgment, which is then complicated by divine compassion.
participants: Assyria and Egypt as political horizons
scenes.setting: prophetic reflection on Israel's history, rebellion, judgment and compassion
scenes.lead_in: Hosea has repeatedly framed Israel's covenant unfaithfulness through intense family and relational metaphors.
scenes.outcome: Care and capability-building imagery is inseparable from grief over rebellion and a movement from threatened judgment toward compassion.
scenes.what_follows: Hosea continues exposing Israel's deception and covenant failure before later restoration promises.
scenes.historical_context: Hosea addresses the northern kingdom of Israel in the context of eighth-century BCE political and covenant crisis.
scenes.literary_context: The chapter deliberately holds parental tenderness and judgment together; the walking image is one element in a larger covenant lament.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Translations vary in details of Hosea's difficult Hebrew, but the parental-care cluster is clear.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage is about YHWH and Israel, not a general therapeutic protocol.
Teaching to walk does not mean all healthy care must withdraw support on a fixed schedule.

scenes.title: The eagle image in the Song of Moses: stirring, hovering, carrying
scenes.summary: Within the Song of Moses, Israel is remembered as found and guarded in a wilderness. Divine care is compared to an eagle stirring its nest, hovering over its young, spreading wings, taking them and carrying them, followed by imagery of YHWH alone leading and abundantly feeding Israel.
scenes.setting: poetic retelling of Israel's origins and dependence within Moses' final song
scenes.lead_in: Deuteronomy 32 summons heaven and earth as witnesses and rehearses YHWH's faithfulness against Israel's coming corruption.
scenes.outcome: Protective carrying belongs to a larger image of guidance, exclusive loyalty and provision.
scenes.what_follows: The song turns sharply to Israel becoming prosperous, forgetting God and provoking judgment.
scenes.historical_context: The Song of Moses is a theological-poetic retrospective embedded in Deuteronomy, not a zoological instruction manual.
scenes.literary_context: Care imagery prepares the contrast with Israel's later ingratitude and rebellion.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The eagle image combines protection and movement; interpreting it specifically as training young to fly goes beyond what every translation states explicitly.
counterreadings_or_limits: The poem does not teach a literal modern release algorithm.
The central subject is divine care for Israel, not interpersonal authority in general.

scenes.title: Hebrews' new and living way into the holy place
scenes.summary: Hebrews moves from its argument about Jesus' priesthood and sacrifice into an exhortation: believers have confidence to enter the holy place by Jesus' blood through a new and living way opened through the curtain, associated with his flesh, and therefore should draw near, hold fast and encourage one another.
scenes.setting: theological exhortation using temple, priesthood and covenant imagery
scenes.lead_in: Hebrews 7-10 has argued that Jesus' priesthood and self-offering provide decisive covenantal access beyond repeated sacrificial rites.
sequence: new and living way through curtain/flesh
scenes.outcome: Access is not merely spatial: it becomes communal practice, perseverance and nearness to God.
scenes.what_follows: A severe warning about deliberate sin and a call to endurance leads into Hebrews' faith examples.
scenes.historical_context: Hebrews reworks Jewish tabernacle/temple and priestly imagery in a distinctively Christian theological argument.
scenes.literary_context: The 'living way' line is the hinge from sacrificial argument to communal exhortation.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The syntax connecting curtain and flesh is interpreted in more than one way; the passage should not be reduced to a generic infrastructure metaphor.
counterreadings_or_limits: Hebrews assigns the mediating access role specifically to Christ.
A modern person functioning as a connector does not thereby become Hebrews' high priest or living way.

scenes.title: Access through Christ in one Spirit to the Father becomes one household and dwelling
scenes.summary: Ephesians addresses formerly alienated Gentiles and describes Christ as making divided groups one. Through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father; strangers become fellow citizens and members of God's household, built together into a holy temple and dwelling of God in the Spirit.
participants: apostles and prophets as foundation imagery
scenes.setting: theological account of reconciliation and communal identity
scenes.lead_in: Ephesians 2 first contrasts death and life by grace, then turns from individual salvation language to the division between Gentile and Jew.
sequence: community built as dwelling in Spirit
scenes.outcome: Access, Spirit, Father, household and dwelling form a relational chain whose endpoint is reconciled communal habitation.
scenes.what_follows: Ephesians 3 develops the Gentile inclusion mystery and Paul's ministry before later ethical exhortation.
scenes.historical_context: The passage addresses identity and reconciliation across Jew/Gentile division in the early Christian movement.
scenes.literary_context: House and temple imagery grows directly out of the reconciliation/access argument rather than standing as an isolated architectural symbol.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The communal temple metaphor is ecclesial and relational; it should not automatically be mapped onto a literal building or neurological structure.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage locates access 'through' Christ and 'in' one Spirit 'to' the Father; these differentiated roles should not be flattened into identical entities.
The house is a reconciled community, not a claim about a modern individual's ownership of humanity.

scenes.title: Zechariah's Branch grows, builds the temple and bears royal-priestly honor
scenes.summary: Zechariah receives silver and gold to make a crown associated with Joshua the high priest, then announces a figure called Branch who will branch out from his place, build YHWH's temple, bear glory and sit/rule on a throne, with counsel of peace between royal and priestly dimensions.
scenes.lead_in: Zechariah's night visions have addressed restoration, priestly cleansing, Zerubbabel and temple rebuilding after exile.
scenes.outcome: Organic growth, temple construction, glory and rule are deliberately compressed into one restoration oracle.
scenes.what_follows: Zechariah turns to questions about fasting and then broader restoration/judgment oracles.
scenes.historical_context: The oracle belongs to Persian-period Judah's temple-restoration setting and is entangled with Joshua/Zerubbabel expectations.
scenes.literary_context: The Branch image is not merely botanical; it moves immediately into building and governance within post-exilic restoration.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Interpretation of Joshua, Branch and royal/priestly relations is debated; later messianic readings should be distinguished from the oracle's post-exilic setting.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not predict the modern Potatoverse.
A generic seed→house→throne sequence is a structural comparison, not fulfillment evidence.

scenes.title: Ephesians' body grows as each connected part works
scenes.summary: Ephesians urges unity while preserving differentiated gifts and roles. Leaders equip the saints for ministry so the body of Christ matures; speaking truth in love, the body grows from Christ as head through joints and ligaments as each part works properly.
scenes.setting: ethical/ecclesial exhortation about unity, gifts and maturity
scenes.lead_in: After three chapters of theological identity and reconciliation, Ephesians turns to how the community should live worthy of that calling.
sequence: growth comes from head through supporting connections
scenes.outcome: Authority and support are distributed toward equipping the whole community for mature contribution rather than concentrating all action in one carrier.
scenes.what_follows: The letter contrasts old and new ways of life and develops concrete ethical practice.
scenes.historical_context: The passage is an ecclesial metaphor for Christian community, unity and differentiated gifts.
scenes.literary_context: Distributed contribution arises inside an argument about unity and maturity, not as a technical theory of decentralized systems.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Translations vary around how supporting joints/ligaments are rendered, but mutual contribution and body growth are central.
counterreadings_or_limits: A church-body metaphor is not a literal engineering architecture.
Distributed function does not imply absence of a head/source; Christ remains the head in the passage.
